title: Otis and Reed Race the Fog
markdown:
Otis the osprey kept a nest like a palace in an ancient oak above Willow Creek, wings wide enough to hold a piece of summer sky. His eyes, river-stone bright, watched the water glitter and the fish flash. Reed the rabbit lived in a snug burrow under the same gnarled roots, fluff soft as a dandelion clock, feet like small lightning when he chose to use them. One lived in air. One lived in earth. Their chats happened on a low branch and a clover patch, voices mixing with the creek’s gurgle.

Days were usually as peaceful as a sleepy kitten: Otis swooping for sparkly fish, Reed munching the juiciest clover, the odd hopping contest with field mice that never quite agreed on the rules. Predictable, if you were being honest. Reed liked predictable. Loud noises and sudden WHOOPS made his paws feel like jelly on a wobbly table.

One breezy afternoon a flutter started in his chest anyway. Whiskers twitched. Nose wiggled. He was looking at his own feet as if they had news when a bright blue flurry crossed the creek.

Rhodri Bluejay landed in a hurry of feathers. “Otis! Reed! Mrs. Meadowsweet needs her calming herbs—the ones that smell of sleepy lavender and leftover sunshine. And look.” He pointed a wing.

A giant fluffy fog was rolling in faster than a runaway saucer, gobbling sunshine as if the day had been a snack. Mrs. Meadowsweet, kindest marsh healer on either bank, lived in a hut on the far side. The herbs were for small creatures who went wobbly when the world turned grey.

Reed’s ears drooped. “That fog looks very thick.”

Otis puffed. “I can fly over it in a blink.” Then his sharp eyes found Reed, who had gone rather pale, and the basket, which was a large honesty for one rabbit. “But Reed. We have to get those herbs there before the hut disappears.”

“We’ll race the fog,” Otis said. “You hop. I’ll spot the smooth patches.” Reed’s tummy jigged. He nodded. Mrs. Meadowsweet was waiting, and waiting is a poor medicine.

Otis swooped low. Reed tied the basket on with a sturdy vine and scrambled onto those broad shoulders. “Hold on, hopper.” A mighty flap, and the oak fell away.

The wind that day was not the usual polite breeze. It nudged them forward and then changed its mind. The fog crept up the banks like a silent grey river, tendrils curious about ankles.

“A lot of air,” puffed Reed, clutching neck feathers. He shut his eyes. What if the grey swallowed the map? What if they became a story the creek told badly? He almost asked to turn back to the burrow that always smelled of earth and not of weather.

A swirl caught them over mid-creek, an invisible giant playing tag. Reed’s fur mussed. He buried his face in Otis’s warm neck and felt the wings rumble, a hug with pinions. He peeked. The far shore was a rumour. Misty ghosts investigated their feet.

They could not stay airborne the whole way with the basket shifting. Otis set Reed on the muddy bank where tree roots snaked like grumpy fingers trying to trip a good deed. Reed hopped, oopsed, hopped again. Mud painted his white socks. Lungs working. A field mouse popped up, saw the fog, and popped down without offering directions. Otis circled, calling just loud enough. “A little left. Smooth patch ahead. Mind the wet stone—the shiny one lies.” Reed’s vine slipped once; he yanked the basket up before a sprig of lavender could take a swim. Otis dropped, righted it with a careful beak, and lifted off again, a dark shape in weather that wanted to be the only character.

The hut showed at last, a small honest square, apron-wave at the edge of the thickest white. Mrs. Meadowsweet’s kind face had a crease in it, the sort that arrives when a kettle is ready and the path is not.

Otis landed with a thump and lowered Reed and the herbs. The fog closed like a fluffy monster finishing its supper. Path to the door: already a rumour.

“You have done wonderfully,” she said. “I need these now, and the path back is going.”

Otis looked at Reed. Reed looked at Otis. Comfort would have been the oak and the burrow and a clover that did not require courage.

“I’ll carry him,” Otis said, and nudged with his beak.

Reed hesitated. He was already wobbly from the first flight. Fog-flying, holding on, trusting a bird who could not see: a large ask for a rabbit whose job was usually clover. He imagined slipping. He imagined Otis turning circles in grey. The air was damp and chilly; the fog whispered as if it had opinions. He took a breath that tasted of lavender from the basket. “Okay.”

He settled between the powerful wings and held the smooth feathers. “Ready?” Otis rumbled. Reed nodded, whiskers busy, eyes bright enough to count.

They went straight into the heart of it. A soft damp cloud tickled noses and made the basket smell twice as lavender. Otis saw only shades of grey and had to trust the feel of current, the memory of the creek’s bend where the willow leans, and the small weight that meant he was not alone. Once the wind shoved them sideways; he corrected without a speech. Reed shut his eyes, then opened them because a closed eye in fog is just more fog. The wings went swish-swish, not scary, a clock you could borrow. Warmth came up through the feathers. Water beaded on whiskers. The wobble thinned. They were not lost. They were a team the fog had not been invited to join.

Then the world had edges again: oak grain, creek glitter, a berry bush that had been waiting without fuss. Sun on their own bank, the colour of an ordinary afternoon that had survived. They landed by Mrs. Meadowsweet’s favourite bush, next to nest and burrow as if the oak had been keeping their places warm.

Otis shook rainbows out of his wings. “We beat the fog.”

Reed hopped down damp and larger somehow, mist still beaded in his guard hairs. He had flown through grey. He had held on. Otis had not dropped the important job, or him. Mrs. Meadowsweet’s herbs were already at work in the hut they could not see; on this bank the berry bush offered a tart congratulations. Being a worrier, Reed found, did not cancel being useful. The clover he tried tasted extra. He told himself it was the sunshine. His toes knew it was also the landing.

Otis thudded beside him, eyes kind. “You were very brave, Reed.”

Reed’s nose twitched. “You were very strong. We make a good team.” He took another mouthful. The creek went on glittering, as if it had never been eaten, and Rhodri Bluejay, somewhere in a clearer tree, was already telling the version with more wings.
